title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Towards a Discipline of Regulation Engineering
content: Prompt engineering improves what LLM agents say. Regulation Engineering governs what they are permitted to do — and this paper formalizes that distinction as a new engineering discipline.LLM agent failure modes are not primarily model capability problems — they are structural regulation problems. Regulation Engineering is the iterative, failure-driven design of behavioral constraints for LLM agent architectures. Unlike prompt engineering, which is ad hoc and model-dependent, or configuration, which adjusts operational parameters, Regulation Engineering treats regulation text as a first-class engineering artifact: discoverable through failure analysis and verifiable through ablation.We ground this claim in the Structured Cognitive Loop (SCL) architecture, where a three-layer regulation hierarchy governs agent behavior: Layer 1 specifies universal behavioral principles, Layer 2 enables external domain injection without core modification, and Layer 3 generates per-cycle contextual constraints at runtime. Through three concrete case studies — premature termination, branch selection error, and Branch Announcement Rule generalization — we demonstrate how specific failure modes drove the discovery and formalization of regulation patterns.We further argue that Regulation Engineering enables three higher-order structural properties: Evidence-Grounding, Accountability Attribution, and Structural Reproducibility. An ablation experiment comparing GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5 (Thinking mode) — models from the same family selected to isolate structural factors from model heterogeneity — validates the independent contribution of each structural layer. Critically, GPT-5.5 Thinking mode, despite superior raw capability, produces systematic behavioral degradation under full regulation and catastrophic over-calling without it: Thinking mode optimizes for reasoning depth, not behavioral accountability. Regulation Engineering is not a supplement to architecture — it is the mechanism that makes architecture behaviorally reliable.
